fact: URA's Ritah Elizabeth Akech said the move to the NIN as the individual tax identifier is being implemented in phases, starting with mapping existing NINs to TINs.
Akech said existing taxpayers can update their details through an account on the URA online portal or at URA service points, and new taxpayers are registered by URA.
Akech said taxpayers give fingerprint consent at a URA service point so URA devices can pull basic biodata from NIRA servers and verify identity against NIRA's records.
Akech said non-individual taxpayers will be issued an Entity Registration Number through the Uganda Registration Services Bureau as their tax identifier.
New Vision reports Uganda has used a 10-digit TIN issued by URA for every taxpayer for over two decades, and the TIN system captured just over 5 million taxpayers per URA's Christine Mirembe.
Mirembe said the government will phase out the TIN for individuals and replace it with the NIN.
Mirembe said the URSB registration number will become the tax identifier for companies.
URA's Christine Mirembe said URA issues a TIN for tax-related transactions such as registering a vehicle or land title.
Mirembe said the transition from TINs to NINs is under way to create a single identifier and improve the accuracy of taxpayer records.
Finance Minister Henry Musasizi said a smaller number of people than hold NINs are captured in the tax register, with the TIN issued by URA.
Cabinet approved use of the NIN as a tax identifier on 31 August 2026, and Musasizi said the NIN and TIN must be interoperable.
The Ministry of Finance says the URA taxpayer register held about 5.7 million records at 30 June 2026, including about 5.4 million individuals.
Uganda Business News reports the Uganda Revenue Authority holds 5.41 million individual taxpayer records and taxpayers log in with their Tax Identification Number.
